blocks.x: Luthier, right? Right. That's what we'll be listening to on the other side of the news. Thank you.
There we have one called Ready Eddie. Barney Begard, do you recognize that young fellow in clarinet?
Yes, I do. Quite a long time ago. A lot of these things were made that I never recognized until I hear them again. Then it dawned on me, well, I did this thing, sure.
Do you have any idea how many records you may have recorded over the years? Oh, not the faintest idea.

You lost count after 5,000 I bet. Oh, easy. I made them all with Duke, I made some of my own, I made some with Freddie Slight, and I made a lot of them with Louie. And I made a lot of different groups, you know, like on the side, what do you call a sideline, you know, one of those deals. And made a lot of studio recordings.

So it's pretty high. You know, we've had a number of people on the show, and we've talked to them about jazz, or swing, or big bands, or whatever you want to call it. And it would seem to me that you would be the man that would know the origin of such terms as jazz. Because you were born originally down there in the Crescent City itself, weren't you?

Yeah, I was born in New Orleans, and they say that's where jazz was born. I mean, of course, a lot of the great guys came out of New Orleans, like Louis Armstrong, and King Oliver, and Buddy Petit, and Buddy Bolden, Lorenzo Teo, Piku, Alphonse Piku. What was the first group? And the Andrei, and people like that.
What was the first group you worked with?

I don't know, we had a little, we were young and we were learning, and some guy couldn't blow his nose on a trumpet and I couldn't blow, they used to call me a snake charmer because I'd grab one note and just hold it till Christmas, you know. And it went all like that until, we used to go around and hear all the good players, you know, and then try to steal what we could from them and then we put it in our memory and we'd go home and start, anytime we'd go home we'd start picking out the instruments and start trying to imitate it or try to copy what they were doing.
Who were some of the people that you were copying at the time? Who, me? Yeah.

I copied anybody I could. Anybody? I used to, I loved Jimmy Noon, and I loved Big I, Louis, and of course I loved my teacher Lorenzo Teo, and I loved Alphonse Piku, and they were about the best, as far as the clarinet is concerned, they were about the best down there.
This was really the experimental, the pioneering stage of music, wasn't it, where no one had been, shall we say, moving in the direction of this kind of music, and these were fellas that were-

No, no, it was a different kind of music altogether. I mean, the people, the guys up north, they didn't, they've never heard anything like that until the musicians from Noon began to migrate, and they went to Chicago, it was the first stop. And then, move on into New York, and things began to happen, and they began to appreciate it.
What was the first recording made that you recall? Your first recording, who was it made with?

It was made with, uh, made in Chicago, with a guy named, uh, My Knee Jones, he was a peg-legged pianist. Mm-hm. And, uh, well, in fact, when I went to Chicago, and I was supposed to go to work with King Alva, it was near the end, and the place where we were going to work, we were supposed to start on the Christmas Eve, and it burned down. Mm-hm. So we were sort of stranded. And this, uh, fellow, My Knee Jones, he was from New Orleans, and he was a writer, composer. And he had little gigs, and he found out that we were starving. So, I was Nicholas and I were a team at that particular time. And he was playing, uh, he'd go around and play at theaters for anything he could get, you know. Mm-hm. So, uh, he would take us out and, uh, say, well, I can't guarantee any salary, but we're gonna play this theater on a percentage. So we'd go out there and come out with 50 cents a piece. I mean, there wasn't nobody in the theater. It was so cool. And so it went on like that until finally we got a good break. Uh, King Alva got a place at the, a job at the plantation. Mm-hm. And they did everything in their power to keep, keeping from bringing a band in there, but he made a triumph, and the people just loved him. And we stayed there for quite some time.
What was it that inspired you to go into music, Marnie Begard?

Me? Well, I wanted to, truthfully, I wanted to be a trumpet player. Really? And, uh, because, and then I could whistle good. So the, the, the old folks, you know, they said, well, the sun is too much wind. You can't blow that kind of horses. I want to try the clarinet. So, uh, I said, okay. So, uh, I said, okay. So, my uncle was a fiddle player, Emil Begard. A fiddle player? Yeah. He used to lead a band. He used to lead Kid Overs band into that. Uh-huh. And, uh, Baby Daz was the clarinetist. And in those, those days, they used to have a, when they played parade or a funeral, they had what they call a, a, an E-flat clarinet. It was real small, you know. Uh-huh. So, by me being small, my uncle borrowed the clarinet from Baby Daz for me to learn on. And that's how it started. Uh-huh. But I was terrible. Wait. Oh, I was awful. It took me quite a while to get straight. And the only thing that got me straight was, uh, you see, I'd put down the clarinet altogether. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Because at that time, uh, soprano sax was kind of popular. And, uh, the music they were writing, like, they'd have, like, the chorus for sax and then change over to clarinet, well, I'd change over to the soprano. I didn't play the clarinet at all. And we had two good clarinetists in there, Albert Nicholas and Darnell Howard. Uh-huh. So they didn't need me at all on the clarinet. That's the way they went until finally, uh, uh, Nick, Albert Nicholas and Darnell, they went to China. I was supposed to go to China and I didn't want to go. So Oliver says to me, he says, hey, didn't you used to play clarinet? I say, yeah, but forget it. Uh-huh. So he says, no. He says, if I buy you one, will you try to play it? I said, well, I got to lose. I said, sure, go ahead. So he bought me old con clarinet and I started woodshedding. And I found out, I discovered I could play more clarinet than I could in my life. Uh-huh. Because I had the idea from the saxophone, you see. And then it blossomed like that. Then I lost all interest in saxophone. I started with the clarinet and that's how it started all over again.

Now you're talking about these marching bands, uh, the bands of New Orleans, you know, going to the funeral and, uh, other occasions and all. Who were some of the people that you might have, uh, marched with? Was Louis Armstrong along with you at the time?

No. I marched with, uh, Buddy Petit. I marched with a guy named Chris Kelly. I marched with, uh, Manuel Perez. Mm-hmm. And, uh, there was a clarinetist, uh, I can't think of his name offhand. Well, he used to play so beautiful at a funeral that all of the women would start crying when they'd start playing. And, uh, but he moved, well, he left New Orleans and he went, and the last time I saw him, that was years ago, he was living in Philadelphia. Mm-hmm. I'll think of his name during the course of the night. But he was real great. He was a great clarinetist.

Well, now, I know that, uh, today most people have an idea of what the Duke Ellington band sounds like. I mean, the minute you first hear the first few notes, you say, that's Duke Ellington. But I'm sure that when we start playing this next one, that, uh, if we weren't to identify the band, that might take them a bit of a time, unless there are real jazz buffs, to identify this sound. Because this one goes back to, I believe, about 1929, 1930, when Duke Ellington was at the Cotton Club. And we have one called, uh, Shout'em and Tilly. You remember this stage? Oh, yeah, I think so. All these things gotta come back to me. We'll go along after.

Because it's been so long. But there were good days, you know, and, uh, when I first joined Duke's band, and he used to arrange so weird, I used to think all these chords were wrong. Yeah. And he and I would have the biggest arguments and everything, but he'd prove it was right. And, uh, that's the way he's been. Of all the bands in the country, everybody could always identify Ellington when he came on the air. Right. And during the Depression, everybody wasn't working. Duke was working. Yeah. All through the Depression. We've never had a bit of trouble at all. Because people knew the band, I mean, and most of the things we played was his tune, though some of the tune of the guys in the band. Yeah. They were all originals. And so we went on.
Let's listen to this one. As we said, Duke Ellington, Cotton Club Band, 1930. Shout them, Antilly. Mm-hm. The End The End The End The End The End
The End The End

segments.title: Opening and counting Bigard's many recordings
segments.summary: Radio host plays a record and asks Bigard if he recognizes himself; he cannot say how many records he made.

segments.title: Born in New Orleans; learning with young players
segments.summary: Bigard names the great New Orleans players and describes learning, holding long notes and imitating good players.

segments.title: Clarinet models in New Orleans and the music's migration north
segments.summary: He copied Jimmie Noone, Big Eye Louis and teacher Lorenzo Tio; New Orleans music spread via Chicago to New York.

segments.title: First recording in Chicago and the burned-down job
segments.summary: First recording was in Chicago with pianist Richard M. Jones; Oliver's job burned down, and he and Nicholas scraped by before Oliver got the Plantation.

segments.title: Wanting trumpet, starting clarinet, switching back under Oliver
segments.summary: Told to play clarinet, he learned on a borrowed E-flat from his uncle's band, drifted to soprano sax, then returned to clarinet when Oliver bought him one.

segments.title: Marching with Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly and Manuel Perez
segments.summary: He names the parade bands he marched with and a clarinetist who made women cry at funerals.

segments.title: Joining Ellington and the band's identifiable sound
segments.summary: Bigard recalls arguing with Duke over his odd chords, the band working through the Depression, then a 1930 Cotton Club record is played.
